label: Out of Taiwan
summary: Austronesian-speaking farmers and voyagers spread from Taiwan through the Philippines towards the Moluccas, ancestors of the Lapita people.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Dates from archaeology and linguistics are approximate (c. 2200 BC Philippines, c. 1500 BC eastern Indonesia).

label: Marianas
summary: First long open-sea crossing in human history, from the Philippines some 2,300 km to Guam and Saipan.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Ancestors of the Chamorro; Micronesian, not Polynesian, but part of the same Austronesian voyaging tradition. c. 1500 BC (Carson).

label: Aegean Bronze Age
summary: Starting world c. 1400 BC: the Aegean coasts and islands, Crete, Rhodes and western Anatolia, with contacts to Cyprus, the Levant coast, the Nile delta and Amarna, and Mycenaean trade points in southern Italy, the Aeolian islands and eastern Sicily.
notes: Extent reconstructed from the archaeological distribution of Mycenaean and Minoan pottery and from Egyptian and Hittite records; known to Greeks orally, not through surviving geographical writing. The Mycenaean and Minoan pages could not be fetched in this session (access blocked); extent from standard accounts.

leader: Lapita culture in the Bismarck Archipelago
label: Lapita: Bismarcks
summary: The Lapita cultural complex, with its dentate-stamped pottery, appears in the Bismarck Archipelago (Mussau, New Britain, New Ireland).
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. c. 1350 to 1300 BC (Denham, Bronk Ramsey and Specht 2012). New Guinea and the Bismarcks had been home to Papuan peoples for over 40,000 years.

label: Lapita: New Caledonia
summary: Lapita voyagers settled the Loyalty Islands and Grande Terre, naming the type site at Lapita (Kone).
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. c. 1100 to 1000 BC.

label: Zhou China
summary: The Yellow River heartland of the Shang and Western Zhou: the Wei valley, the central plain, Shandong and Yan.
notes: Starting world for the china viewpoint.

leader: Lapita crossing into Remote Oceania (Reef and Santa Cruz)
label: Lapita: Santa Cruz
summary: Lapita voyagers passed the inhabited main Solomons to settle the Reef and Santa Cruz Islands, the first step into Remote Oceania.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Nanggu and Nenumbo sites, c. 1000 BC (Sheppard et al.).

label: Lapita: Vanuatu
summary: First settlement of Vanuatu, including the Teouma cemetery on Efate.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Teouma c. 3000 to 2900 BP (Petchey et al.).

label: Lapita: Fiji
summary: Settlement of Fiji from Vanuatu, the gateway to Polynesia; earliest site at Bourewa on Viti Levu.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Bourewa c. 2900 to 2850 BP (Nunn). Route crosses the antimeridian.

label: Lapita: Tonga
summary: First settlement of Tonga at Nukuleka on Tongatapu, the earliest site in Polynesia.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Nukuleka c. 2838 plus or minus 8 BP by U-Th coral dating (Burley et al. 2012).

leader: Lapita settlement of Wallis, Futuna and Samoa
label: Lapita: Samoa
summary: Lapita settlers reached Futuna, Uvea and Samoa (Mulifanua), completing the settlement of West Polynesia.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Mulifanua c. 2800 BP. Then followed the long pause of some 1,800 years in West Polynesia, where Ancestral Polynesian culture formed.

label: Kition
summary: Phoenician settlement at Kition on Cyprus, the first step of Tyre's westward expansion.
notes: Cyprus may have been reached as early as the 11th century BC; Kition as a Phoenician town is usually placed in the 9th century BC.

label: Carthage founded
summary: Tyrians found Carthage on the Gulf of Tunis, opening the central Mediterranean sea route west.
notes: Traditional date 814 BC (Timaeus), accepted range 846 to 813 BC. Exact sailing route is not recorded; this follows the usual Cyprus, south Crete, Malta line.

label: Gadir
summary: Tyrian foundation of Gadir (Cadiz) beyond the Pillars of Heracles, the Phoenician gateway to the Atlantic and the silver of Tartessos.
notes: Tradition says c. 1100 BC; no strata earlier than the 9th century BC have been found, so c. 800 BC is used. Coastal route along North Africa assumed.

label: Sardinia
summary: Phoenician settlements at Caralis, Nora, Sulcis and Tharros along the southern and western coasts of Sardinia.
notes: Sardinia probably colonised in the 9th century BC; individual dates uncertain.

label: Utica
summary: Phoenician colony of Utica on the Tunisian coast.
notes: Traditional foundation 1101 BC; archaeology gives no earlier than the 8th century BC, which is used here.

leader: Euboean colonists of Chalcis and Eretria
label: Pithekoussai
summary: Euboean Greeks settle Pithekoussai (Ischia) and Cumae, the first Greek colonies in Italy.
notes: Pithekoussai at the beginning of the 8th century BC per the page read; Cumae followed.

label: Homeric world
summary: Starting world c. 750 BC: the Aegean, the Hellespont and the entrance to the Black Sea, Sicily and southern Italy, Egypt and the Nile up to Thebes, Phoenicia (Sidon), Cyprus and the Libyan coast, as reflected in the Homeric poems and the first Euboean colonies.
notes: Homer names Egyptian Thebes, Sidon, Cyprus, Libya and Pharos; western places in the Odyssey are partly mythical. Euboean settlement at Pithekoussai (early 8th century BC) is from the Greek colonisation page read; the Homeric geography pages could not be fetched in this session.

label: Lixus
summary: Phoenician colony at Lixus on the Loukkos estuary, first foothold on Africa's Atlantic coast.
notes: Founded 8th or 7th century BC over a Bronze Age settlement; the land was known to its Mauri inhabitants.

label: W Sicily and Malta
summary: Phoenician settlements on Malta and at Motya, Panormus (Palermo) and Solus in western Sicily.
notes: Motya c. 750 BC; Malta settled about the same time.

label: Greek Sicily
summary: Greek colonies ring eastern and southern Sicily: Naxos, Syracuse, Gela, Akragas and Selinus.
notes: Syracuse (Corinthian) 8th century BC per the page read; Naxos 734, Gela 688, Selinus 628 BC are the traditional Thucydidean dates; Akragas (580 BC) is shown on the way.

label: Magna Graecia
summary: Achaean and Spartan colonies at Sybaris, Croton and Taras round the Gulf of Taranto.
notes: Sybaris (Achaean) 8th century BC per the page read; Croton c. 710 and Taras c. 706 BC are traditional dates. Waypoint years follow geography, not foundation order.

label: Byzantium
summary: Megarians found Byzantium and Chalcedon at the Bosporus, the gateway to the Black Sea.
notes: Megara named as mother city on the page read; 667 BC is the traditional date (not given on that page).

label: Ibiza
summary: Settlement of Ebusus (Ibiza) in the Balearics, described as Carthage's first recorded independent action.
notes: c. 650 BC; an earlier Phoenician presence on Ibiza is attested.

label: Mogador
summary: Phoenician trading station on Mogador Island (Essaouira), the southernmost known Phoenician site on the Atlantic.
notes: Page read confirms Phoenician artefacts and a 5th century BC post linked to Hanno but gives no date; the 7th century BC date follows the excavated Phoenician pottery reported in the archaeological literature.

label: Colaeus to Tartessos
summary: A Samian trader driven west beyond the Pillars of Heracles reaches Tartessos, the first recorded Greek visit to Atlantic Spain.
notes: Herodotus 4.152 places it at the time of the Theran settlement on Platea before Cyrene (631 BC), so c. 640 BC. Many scholars think the storm was a cover for a deliberate route. Route reconstructed.

label: Cyrene
summary: Therans under Battus found Cyrene (inland of its port Apollonia), opening Greek knowledge of Libya.
notes: 631 BC per Herodotus and a 4th century BC inscription; first settlement on Platea island.

label: Istros and Olbia
summary: Milesian colonies on the western and northern Black Sea: Apollonia, Istros, Tyras, Berezan and Olbia at the Dnieper-Bug estuary.
notes: Istros, Apollonia and Olbia are Milesian per the page read; dates are the usual archaeological ones (Berezan late 7th century, Olbia 6th century BC).

label: Sinope
summary: Milesians found Sinope on the southern Black Sea coast, base for Pontic expansion.
notes: 7th century BC (some scholars 8th); archaeology of Greek Black Sea settlement begins in the late 7th century BC.

label: Naucratis
summary: Greek trading post of Naucratis on the Canopic Nile, Greece's window on Egypt.
notes: Established by Milesian merchants under Psammetichus I by the mid-7th century BC per the page read. Last leg is up the Canopic branch of the Nile.

leader: Spring and Autumn states of the Yangtze (base)
label: Chu, Wu, Yue
summary: The middle and lower Yangtze states of Chu, Wu and Yue as they entered the Chinese record.

label: Panticapaeum
summary: Greek colonies in Crimea and the Kerch strait (Panticapaeum, Theodosia, Phanagoria), later the Bosporan kingdom.
notes: Panticapaeum is Milesian per the page read; date c. 600 BC is conventional. Chersonesus was founded later (421 BC).

leader: Phoenician crews of Pharaoh Necho II
label: Circumnavigation of Africa
summary: Herodotus reports Phoenicians sent by Necho II sailed from the Red Sea round Libya (Africa) and back through the Pillars in three years.
notes: Herodotus 4.42; reign of Necho II 610 to 595 BC. Disputed: Herodotus doubted the report that the sun was on their right, which modern readers take as evidence of rounding the Cape. If real, its geography did not enter later Greek maps (Ptolemy thought it impossible), so it is marked as knowledge effectively lost.

label: Massalia
summary: Phocaeans found Massalia (Marseille) near the Rhone mouth, with Alalia on Corsica and later Elea.
notes: Massalia c. 600 BC, Alalia c. 565 BC; years here follow geography. Herodotus credits the Phocaeans as the first Greeks to make long voyages to the Adriatic, Tyrrhenia and Spain.

label: Trapezus and Phasis
summary: Colonies along the eastern Black Sea at Amisos, Trapezus, Phasis in Colchis and Dioscurias.
notes: Trapezus was a Sinopean colony; Phasis and Dioscurias are Milesian foundations of the 6th century BC (dates not given on pages read). Colchis was the land of the Argonaut legend.

label: Emporion and Tartessos
summary: Phocaeans found Emporion and trade down the Iberian coast to Tartessos, whose king Arganthonios befriended them.
notes: Emporion 575 BC. The Massaliote Periplus describes trade to Gades and Tartessus; Carthage probably closed the strait to Greeks after c. 500 BC.

label: Euthymenes
summary: A Massaliote voyage down Africa's Atlantic coast to a great crocodile-filled river, probably the Senegal.
notes: Dated early 6th century BC on the Euthymenes page and late 6th century BC on the Massalia page; c. 550 BC used. He took the river for the Nile. Only fragments survive (Seneca, Aetius).

label: Scylax down the Indus
summary: A Carian Greek in Persian service sails down the Indus to the sea, the first Greek account of India.
notes: Herodotus 4.44, reign of Darius I (Scylax fl. 510s BC). Start at Caspatyrus (location unknown, near Gandhara; Bivar suggested the Kabul river near Peshawar).

label: Scylax round Arabia
summary: Scylax sails west from the Indus mouth and round Arabia to Suez, 30 months in all.
notes: Exact coastal route not recorded.

label: Hecataeus' map
summary: World of Hecataeus' Periodos Ges c. 500 BC: a coastal circuit from the Pillars of Heracles clockwise round the Mediterranean and Black Sea to Atlantic Morocco, with Egypt and the Persian heartland along the Royal Road.
notes: Hecataeus improved Anaximander's map; his work covered Scythia, Persia, India, Egypt and Nubia, partly from hearsay. India is lit by the Scylax entry rather than here. The Royal Road line is approximate.

label: Hanno
summary: Carthaginian fleet of 60 ships founds colonies on Atlantic Morocco and sails down West Africa past the Senegal toward a burning mountain and the 'Gorillai'.
notes: 5th century BC. Identifications: Thymiaterion near Mehdya; Kerne perhaps Herne island (Dakhla) or Mogador; farthest point disputed from southern Morocco to Sierra Leone (Kakoulima), Mount Cameroon or Gabon. Senegal is the broad consensus minimum; ended here at Sherbro (Sierra Leone). Interpreters from the Lixitae accompanied the fleet.

label: Himilco
summary: Carthaginian voyage north along Atlantic Iberia to the tin lands of the Oestrymnides (Brittany), perhaps the British Isles.
notes: Early 5th century BC, known only through Pliny and Avienus' Ora maritima; route and farthest point uncertain (Ireland suggested speculatively).

label: Herodotus in Egypt
summary: Herodotus travels up the Nile to Elephantine and records Egypt and hearsay of Meroe and Nubia beyond.
notes: Later 450s BC per Cartledge's estimate; he also visited Cyrenaica. Relied on Egyptian priests as informants.

label: Herodotus in Asia
summary: Herodotus' travels in Syria and Mesopotamia, possibly to Babylon and Susa, describing the Persian empire.
notes: Babylon is uncertain; Herodotus says he visited Tyre (Histories 2.44). Route reconstructed.

label: Herodotus in Scythia
summary: Herodotus visits the Black Sea and the Scythian coast to the Borysthenes (Dnieper), gathering the first detailed account of the steppe peoples.
notes: Dates are guesses (c. 450 to 430 BC); Olbia is the usual inference for his base, not named on the page read.

leader: Cyrus the Younger and the Ten Thousand (Xenophon)
label: Anabasis: march up
summary: The march of the Ten Thousand from Sardis through Cilicia and down the Euphrates to Cunaxa near Babylon.
notes: 401 BC. Stage list from Xenophon's Anabasis; intermediate locations approximate.

label: Anabasis: retreat
summary: Retreat of the Ten Thousand up the Tigris, through the Carduchian mountains and Armenian winter to the Black Sea at Trapezus.
notes: Winter 401 to 400 BC; 'Thalatta! Thalatta!' at Mount Theches. Xenophon records local guides, including an Armenian village headman.

label: Anabasis: coast
summary: The Ten Thousand move west along the Pontic coast by ship and on foot via Cotyora, Sinope and Heraclea to Byzantium.
notes: Coast was already known from the Greek colonies; included for completeness of the Anabasis.

label: Alexander: Danube
summary: Alexander's Balkan campaign across the Haemus to the Danube and into Illyria.
notes: Return through the Haemus to Illyria and Thebes follows a different route.

label: Alexander: Asia Minor to Egypt
summary: Alexander crosses to Asia, wins at the Granicus and Issus, takes Tyre and Gaza and enters Egypt, founding Alexandria and visiting Siwa.

label: Alexander: Mesopotamia and Persia
summary: Alexander marches across Mesopotamia to Gaugamela, takes Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, then Ecbatana.

label: Alexander: Iran to Central Asia
summary: Pursuit of Darius and Bessus through Parthia, Aria, Drangiana and Arachosia, over the Hindu Kush to Bactria and Sogdiana as far as the Jaxartes.
notes: Local guides and rulers supplied routes over the Hindu Kush. Positions of Hecatompylos and Artacoana approximate.

label: Alexander: into India
summary: Alexander crosses the Hindu Kush into the Kabul valley and Swat, crosses the Indus, defeats Porus on the Hydaspes and reaches the Hyphasis (Beas).
notes: Taxiles of Taxila allied with Alexander and provided guides and elephants.

label: Alexander: down the Indus
summary: Fleet and army descend the Hydaspes, Acesines and Indus to Patala and the Indus delta.
notes: Fleet built near the Hydaspes; Alexandria-on-the-Indus founded at the Acesines confluence.

label: Alexander: Gedrosia
summary: Return through the Gedrosian desert (Makran) and Carmania to Persepolis, Susa, Opis and Babylon.
notes: Heavy losses in the Gedrosian desert. Met Nearchus at Salmous in Carmania.

label: Craterus via Arachosia
summary: Craterus leads the heavy troops and elephants from the Indus through the Bolan pass, Arachosia and Drangiana to Carmania.
notes: Route from Arrian's Anabasis; not described on the page read. Exact pass uncertain.

label: Nearchus
summary: Nearchus sails the fleet from the Indus along the Makran coast and up the Persian Gulf to the Tigris mouth, charting the route by sea.
notes: Places named include Morontobara (Manora), Bagisara (Ormara), Carnine (Astola), Gwadar, Harmozeia, Qeshm and Bushehr. A Gedrosian pilot, Hydraces, guided the fleet from Mosarna (Arrian, Indica).

label: Pytheas: Britain and Thule
summary: Pytheas sails from Massalia out of the Mediterranean, round Brittany and Britain and north to Thule, giving the first account of the British Isles and the Arctic north.
notes: c. 325 BC. How he passed the Carthaginian blockade is unknown (an overland route to the Loire is possible). Thule is uncertain (Norway favoured on latitude; Iceland, Shetland, Faroes also proposed); Berrice, his departure point for Thule, may be Lewis. Order of the Britain circuit reconstructed.

label: Pytheas: amber coast
summary: Pytheas visits the amber coast of northern Europe (Abalus) and the Guiones, perhaps turning back at the Vistula.
notes: Whether the amber estuary lay on the North Sea or Baltic is disputed; some treat this as a second voyage.

label: Megasthenes
summary: Seleucid envoy Megasthenes travels from Arachosia through the Punjab and down the Ganges plain to Pataliputra, writing the Indica.
notes: Date disputed (after c. 303 BC most likely). Route through the Punjab and along the Yamuna and Ganges inferred from his descriptions.

label: Patrocles on the Caspian
summary: Seleucid admiral Patrocles explores the Caspian Sea, wrongly concluding it was a gulf of the outer Ocean.
notes: Active c. 312 to 270 BC; extent of his voyage not recorded, here the southern and south-eastern shores.

label: Tanais
summary: Bosporan Greek trading city of Tanais at the mouth of the Don, the edge of the Greek world toward the steppe.
notes: Tanais is listed among Greek Black Sea colonies on the page read but without a date; founded in the 3rd century BC by standard accounts. The Sea of Azov (Maeotis) was known to Herodotus earlier.

label: Cisalpine Gaul
summary: Rome conquers the Po valley after Telamon, founding Placentia, Cremona, Bononia and Aquileia.
notes: Polybius (Histories book 2) is the main narrative. The Cisalpine Gaul page could not be fetched in this session; dates are standard (Telamon 225, Clastidium 222, Placentia and Cremona 218, Bononia 189, Aquileia 181 BC).

label: Qin empire
summary: The unified Qin empire with Sichuan, Lingnan, Liaodong and the Ordos frontier of the Great Wall.
notes: Fujian (Minyue) and the Red River delta were tributary or briefly held; full Han control followed in -111.

leader: Gnaeus and Publius Cornelius Scipio, Scipio Africanus
label: Scipios in Spain
summary: Roman armies land at Emporion and fight Carthage down eastern and southern Spain to Carthago Nova, Baecula, Ilipa and Gades.
notes: Second Punic War. The Scipio brothers fell in 211 BC; Scipio Africanus took Carthago Nova in 209 BC.

label: Cato in Spain
summary: Cato subdues Hispania Citerior north of the Ebro, marches into Turdetania and the Celtiberian interior at Segestica (Siguenza).
notes: Landing at Emporiae and wintering at Tarraco from the page read; inland route between Turdetania and Segestica reconstructed.

label: Gracchus in Celtiberia
summary: Gracchus campaigns in the Ebro valley and Celtiberian plateau, founding Gracchurris and making treaties with the Celtiberians.
notes: Dates and places from standard accounts (Livy); not covered by the portion of the page that could be read.

label: Lucullus in the Meseta
summary: Lucullus pushes west across the Duero plateau against the Vaccaei at Cauca, Intercatia and Pallantia, with Scipio Aemilianus serving under him.
notes: From Appian's Iberica via standard accounts; not covered by the portion of the page that could be read.

label: Polybius' Atlantic voyage
summary: After the fall of Carthage, Polybius explores Africa's Atlantic coast with a fleet lent by Scipio Aemilianus.
notes: Pliny (5.9) lists places he passed; the turning point is unknown. Afterwards he went to Spain.

label: Zhang Qian
summary: First Chinese envoy to the west: reached Dayuan (Ferghana), Kangju, the Yuezhi and Daxia (Bactria), and reported on Parthia and India.
notes: Held by the Xiongnu for about ten years each way; accompanied by the Xiongnu-born guide Ganfu (Tangyi Fu). Route reconstructed.

label: Hexi Corridor
summary: Han armies took the Hexi Corridor from the Xiongnu and founded the four commanderies to Dunhuang and the Jade Gate.

label: Zhang Qian: Wusun
summary: Embassy to the Wusun of the Ili and Issyk Kul region; his deputies went on to Dayuan, Kangju, the Yuezhi, Daxia, Anxi (Parthia) and Shendu.

label: Eudoxus to India
summary: Eudoxus, guided by a shipwrecked Indian sailor, sails from Egypt to India and back, and on a second voyage is blown down the Somali coast.
notes: First voyage c. 118 BC with an Indian pilot; second 116 BC. Indian landfall unspecified; later attempts from Gades to sail round Africa failed and he vanished after c. 105 BC.

label: Eudoxus
summary: First Greek voyage on the monsoon route straight across the Arabian Sea from the Red Sea to India.
notes: Guided on the first voyage by a shipwrecked Indian sailor rescued in the Red Sea (Poseidonius via Strabo). Indian and Arab sailors knew the monsoon long before. Second voyage 116 BC wrecked on the Horn of Africa coast on return. Indian landfall uncertain; west Indian coast assumed.

label: Nanyue, Jiaozhi
summary: Conquest of Nanyue added Lingnan, Hainan and the Red River delta, with Rinan commandery reaching central Vietnam.

label: Eudoxus (Atlantic)
summary: Attempt to sail from Gades round Africa down the Atlantic coast of Morocco; turned back, a later attempt vanished.
notes: Bocchus I of Mauretania refused support; second attempt never heard of after c. 100 BC. Southern limit unknown.

label: Lelang
summary: Han armies took Wanggeom (Pyongyang) and set up the Four Commanderies including Lelang in north Korea.

leader: Li Guangli (War of the Heavenly Horses)
label: Ferghana war
summary: Han army crossed the Tarim and the Tian Shan to besiege Ershi, capital of Dayuan in the Ferghana valley.

leader: Han envoys to Huangzhi (Book of Han)
label: Han sea route to India
summary: Book of Han itinerary from Rinan and Hepu along Indochina to Dulu and Huangzhi (probably Kanchipuram) and Yichengbu (Sri Lanka).
notes: Route reconstructed: the text may imply a portage across the Kra isthmus; Huangzhi is identified with Kanchipuram by most scholars.

label: Pompey
summary: Roman army pursuing Mithridates crossed Armenia into Iberia and Albania (Georgia, Azerbaijan) and reached the Phasis, bringing the Caucasus into Roman knowledge.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Pompey turned back about three days short of the Caspian.

label: Caesar in Gaul
summary: Caesar's eight-year conquest mapped all of Gaul from the Alps to the Channel and the Rhine, with first-hand descriptions of Gaulish and German peoples.
notes: Route of the Gallic Wars (Bibracte, Vesontio, Belgica, Veneti, Rhine bridges 55 and 53 BC, Avaricum, Gergovia, Alesia, Uxellodunum) from Caesar's Commentarii; Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify.

label: Caesar to Britain
summary: First Roman crossing to Britain, landing on the Kent coast between Hythe and Sandwich.
notes: Embarked from Portus Itius in the land of the Morini (probably near Boulogne).

label: Caesar in Britain
summary: Second invasion pushed inland across the Stour and the Thames to Cassivellaunus' stronghold, giving Rome its first description of inland Britain.
notes: Landing probably Ebbsfleet in Pegwell Bay; Thames crossing point unknown; stronghold possibly Wheathampstead. Guided partly by the Trinovantes under Mandubracius.

label: Hippalus
summary: Credited with the direct open-sea crossing to south India on the south-west monsoon, making Muziris a regular Roman port.
notes: Date uncertain (probably 1st century BC). The Periplus credits him with the direct route; Pliny names the wind after him. Indian and Arab mariners used the monsoon earlier.

label: Aelius Gallus
summary: Roman army landed at Leuke Kome and marched six months down western Arabia to besiege Marib, bringing back the first Roman eyewitness geography of Arabia Felix.
notes: Misled (Strabo says) by the Nabataean guide Syllaeus. Fleet from Cleopatris (Suez) to Leuke Kome; retreat via Egra to Myos Hormos. Strabo, his friend, wrote the account.

label: Petronius
summary: Punitive campaign up the Nile through Lower Nubia to Napata, the Kushite royal city, after Kushite raids on Syene.
notes: Cities taken include Pselchis, Primis (Qasr Ibrim) and Napata. Opponent: the Kandake Amanirenas. Peace with Augustus at Samos c. 21/20 BC.

label: Balbus
summary: Campaign into the Fezzan that captured fifteen Garamantian settlements, the first Roman army deep in the Sahara.
notes: Pliny lists the places taken (Cydamus/Ghadames, Garama); route via Ghadames is a reconstruction. Triumph celebrated 19 BC.

label: Juba II
summary: Juba II's expedition to the Fortunate Isles (Canary Islands), reported by Pliny, put the Canaries on the Roman map.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Juba also sent people to Mogador (Iles Purpuraires). Exact date unknown (between c. 25 BC and AD 23).

label: Drusus fleet
summary: First Roman fleet in the North Sea: down the Rhine and the Fossa Drusiana through Lake Flevo to the Frisian coast and the land of the Chauci.
notes: Fossa Drusiana canal linked Rhine and IJssel; exact canal course disputed.

label: Drusus to the Elbe
summary: Drusus marched from the Lippe to the Weser (11 BC) and from Mainz through the Chatti and Cherusci to the Elbe (9 BC), the furthest east any Roman army had gone in Germany.
notes: Exact point on the Elbe unknown (often placed near Magdeburg). Drusus died on the return march.

label: Parthian Stations
summary: Greek itinerary of caravan stations across the Parthian empire, from the Euphrates to Arachosia (Kandahar), possibly written for Augustus' grandson Gaius Caesar.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify.

label: Fleet round Jutland
summary: The Roman fleet sailed past the Elbe mouth up the coast of Jutland to the land of the Cimbri and the Skaw, glimpsing the Kattegat and the Baltic beyond.
notes: Augustus (Res Gestae 26) and Velleius Paterculus describe it; the northern limit (Skagen) is suggested, not certain. The fleet also sailed up the Elbe to meet Tiberius' army (see tiberius-elbe-5).

label: Tiberius to the Elbe
summary: Tiberius' army marched through the Chauci and Langobardi to the lower Elbe, where it met the fleet.

label: Germanicus
summary: Germanicus moved his army by a fleet of about a thousand ships from the Rhine through Lake Flevo to the Ems before marching to the Weser; the fleet was wrecked by a North Sea storm on return.
notes: Battles of Idistaviso and the Angrivarian Wall on the Weser (AD 16). Tacitus says some storm-driven ships reached Britain and remote islands.

label: Suetonius over the Atlas
summary: First Roman army to cross the Atlas mountains, reaching the desert river Ger beyond; Pliny quotes his description.
notes: Pliny: about ten days to the summit, then to the river Ger through black dust deserts. River Ger possibly the Oued Guir; route a reconstruction.

label: Periplus: Africa
summary: Greek merchant's handbook describing every port down the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa to Rhapta on the Tanzanian coast, the furthest south Roman knowledge reached.
notes: Ports: Berenice, Ptolemais Theron, Adulis, Avalites, Malao, Mosyllon, Aromata (Guardafui), Opone, Menuthias, Rhapta. Rhapta's site is unknown (Pangani or Rufiji area). Date mid 1st century AD most accepted.

label: Periplus: Arabia & India
summary: The Periplus describes the incense coast of Arabia, the Indus port of Barbarikon, Barygaza, the Malabar pepper ports of Muziris and Nelcynda, Roman-traded Poduke (Arikamedu) and the Ganges mouth.
notes: Ports: Muza, Eudaemon Arabia (Aden), Kane, Moscha Limen, Omana, Barbarikon, Barygaza, Muziris, Nelcynda, Komar, Poduke (Arikamedu, where Roman amphorae and Arretine ware were excavated), Ganges. The author knew Chryse and Thina (China) by hearsay only. Circuit of Sri Lanka added for mapping; the text mentions Palaesimundu (Taprobane).

leader: Roman knight sent by Julianus (Nero's games)
label: Amber road
summary: A Roman eques travelled from Carnuntum along the Amber Road to the Baltic coast to buy amber, as Pliny reports.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Pliny gives about 600 miles from Carnuntum. Coast reached probably Sambia or the Vistula mouth.

label: Nero's Nile party
summary: Party sent by Nero up the Nile past Meroe and up the White Nile to the impassable swamps of the Sudd.
notes: Seneca (who spoke to the men) and Pliny. Helped by the Kushite king of Meroe with guides and letters to rulers upstream. Claims that they reached Uganda are disputed.

label: Ban Chao
summary: Thirty years restoring Han power over the Tarim kingdoms, from Shanshan and Khotan to Kashgar, Kucha and Karashahr.

label: Agricola
summary: Agricola's campaigns carried Roman armies through northern Britain beyond the Forth and Tay to the battle of Mons Graupius in north-east Scotland.
notes: Known from Tacitus' Agricola. Mons Graupius usually dated 83 or 84 and placed near Bennachie (site disputed); the fetched page gives c. 86, Tacitus' chronology suggests 83/84.

label: Fleet round Britain
summary: Agricola's fleet sailed round the north of Britain, proving it an island, subdued the Orkneys and sighted Thule (probably Shetland).
notes: Tacitus gives no route; the course round the north and down the west side to the Clyde is a reconstruction. Return harbour (portus Trucculensis) unknown.

label: Septimius Flaccus
summary: Roman commander who marched from Garama three months south into the land of the 'Ethiopians', as reported by Marinus of Tyre via Ptolemy.
notes: The fetched pages only allude to 'Flaccus's success'; date (c. AD 86, after the Nasamones revolt) and southern endpoint (Tibesti region assumed) are uncertain.

label: Julius Maternus
summary: Roman traveller who accompanied the Garamantian king four months south from Garama to Agisymba, a land of rhinoceroses, probably near Lake Chad.
notes: Known from Marinus of Tyre via Ptolemy. Led by the Garamantian king. Agisymba placed near Lake Chad or the Bahr Salamat/Bahr Aouk in Chad; the Kawar route is a reconstruction.

label: Gan Ying
summary: Sent to reach Da Qin (Rome), he crossed Parthia to the sea at Tiaozhi (probably the head of the Persian Gulf) and turned back.
notes: Route and the identity of Tiaozhi are disputed; Parthian sailors reportedly discouraged him.

label: Maes Titianus
summary: Agents of the Macedonian merchant Maes Titianus travelled the Silk Road from the Euphrates through Parthia and Bactria to the Stone Tower and on to Sera, the silk capital; their distances reached Ptolemy via Marinus of Tyre.
notes: Date uncertain: c. AD 100 is commonly given (linked to a Han record of Western visitors), but late 1st century BC is also proposed. Stone Tower location disputed (Daraut-Kurgan in the Alai valley or Tashkurgan). Sera assumed to be Luoyang. Relied on Parthian, Sogdian and Chinese intermediaries.

label: Trajan to the Gulf
summary: Trajan's Parthian war took a Roman army down the Tigris past Ctesiphon to Charax Spasinou and the Persian Gulf.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify.

label: Ptolemy's world
summary: Ptolemy's Geography (c. 150) gave coordinates for some 8,000 places from Ireland and the Canaries to the Silk Road, India, Sri Lanka and the Golden Chersonese, summing up Roman knowledge.
notes: Base area: Britain, Ireland, Orkney/Thule, Germania to the Vistula, southern Scandia, Sarmatia to the Volga, the Caspian, Parthia and the Silk Road to the Tarim, India, Taprobane, the Golden Chersonese, East Africa to Rhapta, the Nile to Meroe and the Fezzan. Built from Marinus of Tyre, Maes Titianus' itinerary and merchants' reports. Geography page itself not fetched.

leader: Embassy of 'Andun' (Marcus Aurelius) to Han China
label: Roman embassy 166 (sea)
summary: Men claiming to come from the Roman emperor 'Andun' (Antoninus) reached China by sea through Rinan in central Vietnam, the first recorded direct Roman contact with China.
notes: Known only from the Chinese Hou Hanshu; probably private merchants. Route via the Strait of Malacca is assumed. Ptolemy also reports a sailor Alexander reaching Kattigara beyond the Golden Chersonese.

leader: Embassy of 'Andun' (Marcus Aurelius) to Han China
label: Roman embassy 166 (land)
summary: Overland stage of the 166 embassy from Rinan through Jiaozhi to the Han court at Luoyang, where it presented ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell to Emperor Huan.
notes: Route between Rinan and Luoyang is a reconstruction.

leader: Wei envoys to the Wa (Weizhi Wajinden)
label: Wei envoys to Wa
summary: Embassies between Daifang and Queen Himiko of Yamatai, giving the first Chinese itinerary to Tsushima, Iki and Kyushu.
notes: Earlier contacts with the Wa date from 57 AD; the location of Yamatai is disputed.

label: Kang Tai to Funan
summary: Wu envoys to Funan in the Mekong delta, whose reports described Funan and lands as far as India.

label: Egeria
summary: Pilgrim Egeria's letters describe Sinai, the Holy Land, Mount Nebo, Edessa and Harran in detail for readers in the far west of Europe.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Guided by local monks and clergy at each holy site.

label: Faxian: overland
summary: Overland across the Taklamakan and the Pamirs to Gandhara and the Buddhist holy places of the Ganges, the first full Chinese account of India.

label: Faxian: by sea
summary: From Tamralipti to Sri Lanka (two years), then via Yepoti (Java or Sumatra) home to the Shandong coast at Laoshan.
notes: Identification of Yepoti and the route through the archipelago are uncertain.

label: Madagascar
summary: Voyagers from southeast Borneo (Ma'anyan-related) settled Madagascar across the Indian Ocean, mixing with East Africans.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Austronesian, not Polynesian. Dates (c. AD 500 to 900) and route are uncertain; may have followed the coasts of South Asia and East Africa instead.

leader: St Brendan of Clonfert (Navigatio Sancti Brendani)
label: St Brendan (legend)
summary: Legendary voyage of St Brendan to islands in the northern Ocean (perhaps the Hebrides, Faroes and Iceland), written down c. 900 and widely read in medieval Europe.
notes: LEGEND: the Navigatio is a literary work; no route can be reconstructed and 'St Brendan's Isle' later wandered across Atlantic maps. Only the northern islands most often suggested are plotted. Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify.

label: Cosmas
summary: Alexandrian merchant whose Christian Topography (c. 550) describes Adulis, Aksum, Socotra, the pepper coast of Male and Taprobane (Sri Lanka) as a hub of Indian Ocean trade.
notes: He certainly visited Adulis and Aksum (c. 522 to 525); whether he reached India and Sri Lanka himself is not certain. Also heard of Tzinista (China).

label: Zemarchus
summary: Byzantine envoy who travelled to the court of the Turkic khagan Istemi in the Tian Shan, and whose report described the steppe route north of the Caspian.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Accompanied by the Sogdian envoy Maniakh; route out uncertain, return via the Volga, the Caspian steppe and the Caucasus.

leader: Arabia at the rise of Islam (base)
label: Arabia
summary: The Arabian peninsula, its Red Sea and Gulf coasts and caravan towns, the home world of the first Muslim community.
notes: Starting world for the islamic viewpoint; Arabian trade networks already linked Yemen, Syria and the Gulf before Islam.

label: Xuanzang: outbound
summary: Slipped out of Tang China, crossed the Tian Shan to the Western Turkic khagan at Suyab, then Samarkand, Balkh, Bamiyan and Gandhara to Kashmir.

label: Xuanzang: India circuit
summary: Studied at Nalanda and travelled around India from Bengal and Kamarupa to Kanchipuram, the Deccan, Gujarat and Sind.
notes: Order of the southern and western circuit is reconstructed from the Records; the Kamarupa visit was in 642/643.

leader: Rashidun conquests of Syria, Iraq and Egypt (base)
label: Syria, Iraq, Egypt
summary: Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia and Egypt as conquered by the Rashidun armies between 634 and 642.

label: Wang Xuance
summary: Tang envoy to King Harsha who used the new Tibet and Nepal road; in 648 he led Tibetan and Nepalese troops into north India.
notes: Three or four missions (643, 647 to 648, 657 to 661); the Tibet-Nepal route followed the Tang-Tibetan marriage alliance.

label: Xuanzang: return
summary: Home over the Hindu Kush, Badakhshan, the Wakhan and the Pamirs to Kashgar and Khotan, reaching Chang'an in 645.

label: Iran
summary: The former Sasanian lands of Iran, Khurasan and the Caucasus brought into the caliphate by 651.
notes: Derbent and the eastern Caucasus were contested with the Khazars into the 8th century.

label: Yijing
summary: Sailed from Guangzhou to Srivijaya (Palembang), Malayu and Kedah and across the Bay of Bengal to Tamralipti, recording the maritime Buddhist world.
notes: Studied at Nalanda 675 to 685 and lived at Srivijaya until 695 on the return.

label: Maghreb
summary: Ifriqiya and the Maghreb to the Atlantic, conquered between the fall of Carthage (698) and about 710.
notes: Zawila in the Fezzan and Sijilmasa entered the Arab network in the 8th century.

label: Irish monks to the Faroes
summary: Irish hermits settled the Faroe Islands about a century before the Norse, as Dicuil records.
notes: Date approximate; Dicuil says the hermits had lived there about a hundred years before Norse raiders drove them out.

label: al-Andalus
summary: Most of the Iberian peninsula and Septimania (Narbonne, 719 to 759) under Umayyad rule.

label: Transoxiana, Sind
summary: Transoxiana (Bukhara, Samarkand, Ferghana) taken by Qutayba ibn Muslim and Sind to Multan by Muhammad ibn Qasim, 705 to 715.

label: Gao Xianzhi: Pamirs
summary: Led a Tang army over the Pamirs and the Darkot pass to Little Balur (Gilgit) in 747, then west to defeat at Talas in 751.

label: Du Huan
summary: Captured at Talas, he lived in the Abbasid world and his Jingxingji gave the first Chinese eyewitness description of the Arabs at Kufa.
notes: He also described Molin, perhaps in North Africa or Aksum; he returned by sea to Guangzhou in 762.

leader: Jia Dan (route from Guangzhou to the Arab lands)
label: Jia Dan sea route
summary: Tang geographer Jia Dan's itinerary of the sea route from Guangzhou through the Strait of Malacca, Sri Lanka and India to the Euphrates mouth and Baghdad.
notes: Compiled from Tang records and foreign envoys c. 785 to 805; also mentions the east African coast.

label: Papar to Iceland
summary: Irish clerics lived in Thule (Iceland) from February to August 795 and sailed a day north to the frozen sea; Dicuil wrote it down in 825.
notes: Dicuil, De mensura orbis terrae (825). The papar were met by Norse settlers (Ari Thorgilsson); place names such as Papey in the east support landfall there. Citation replaced with the English Wikipedia pages; dates not rechecked against them.

label: Charlemagne's embassy
summary: Charlemagne's embassy to Harun al-Rashid in Baghdad; the sole survivor Isaac returned via Ifriqiya with the elephant Abul-Abbas.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Outward route unrecorded (assumed via Egypt and Syria); return via Kairouan and Porto Venere is in the Frankish Annals.

leader: Varangian Rus' (route from the Varangians to the Greeks)
label: Varangians to Byzantium
summary: Norse traders and warriors opened the river road from the Baltic by the Neva, Lake Ladoga, Novgorod and the Dnieper rapids to the Black Sea and Constantinople, attacked in 860.
notes: Rhos envoys reached the Frankish court in 839 (Annals of St Bertin); attack on Constantinople 860; the Dnieper rapids are named in Norse and Slavic by Constantine VII (De Administrando Imperio, c. 952). Relied on Slavic and Finnic peoples along the rivers.

label: Sulaiman the Merchant
summary: First surviving Arabic account of the sea route from Siraf via Kulam Mali, the Nicobars, Kalah and Champa to Khanfu (Guangzhou).
notes: Account compiled 851 and expanded by Abu Zayd al-Sirafi c. 916; authorship by 'Sulaiman' is debated.

label: Gardar
summary: Gardar sailed right round Iceland, proving it an island, and wintered at Husavik.
notes: c. 860. Was heading for the Hebrides and was storm-driven north. His man Nattfari stayed behind at Nattfaravik. Citation replaced with the English Wikipedia pages; dates not rechecked against them.

label: Naddodd
summary: Norse sailor blown off course to the Faroes who reached east Iceland and named it Snaeland.
notes: Date not given in the source (traditionally c. 850 to 860); landing in the eastern fjords (Reydarfjordur) per Landnamabok. Citation replaced with the English Wikipedia pages; dates not rechecked against them.

label: Floki
summary: Floki followed his ravens to Iceland, wintered at Vatnsfjordur in the Westfjords and gave the island its name.
notes: Year unclear (c. 865 to 870). Shetland and Faroe stops from the Landnamabok tradition. Citation replaced with the English Wikipedia pages; dates not rechecked against them.

leader: Ibn Khordadbeh (Book of Roads and Kingdoms)
label: Ibn Khordadbeh: Khurasan road
summary: The Abbasid post road from Baghdad through Khurasan to Transoxiana and the Turkic steppe, with stages and distances.
notes: Ibn Khordadbeh was director of posts in Jibal; the book dates c. 846 to 885.

leader: Ibn Khordadbeh (sea route to China and al-Sila)
label: Ibn Khordadbeh: al-Sila
summary: First Arabic mention of al-Sila (Silla, Korea) at the far end of the sea route along the China coast.
notes: Route north of Khanfu is reconstructed; Ibn Khordadbeh also names Waqwaq.

label: Radhanites
summary: The northern Radhanite trade route from the land of the Franks through the Slav lands and Khazar Itil to Transoxiana and China.
notes: Ibn Khordadbeh lists four Radhanite routes; this is the northern one and the stations between are reconstructed.

label: Wulfstan
summary: Seven days' sail from Hedeby to Truso at the Vistula mouth, describing the Wendish coast, the Danish and Swedish islands and the Aestii, recorded for King Alfred.
notes: Route starts at the Schlei mouth (Hedeby lies up the Schlei) and ends at the entrance of the Vistula Lagoon (Truso, near Elblag, lies inside). Inserted in the Old English Orosius. Islands passed on the left: Langeland, Lolland, Falster, Scania, Bornholm, Blekinge, Möre, Öland, Gotland.

label: al-Ya'qubi: Kanem
summary: Earliest Arabic account of the Fezzan route from Zawila to Kanem near Lake Chad, also naming Kawkaw (Gao) and Ghana.
notes: Compiled from merchants; stations (Bilma) are reconstructed.

label: Ohthere to the White Sea
summary: Ohthere sailed round the North Cape and along the Kola coast into the White Sea to the land of the Beormas, the first known account of the European Arctic coast.
notes: Told by Ohthere at the court of Alfred the Great (c. 890) and inserted in the Old English Orosius. He met Sami (Finnas) and Terfinnas; Bjarmaland usually placed at the Dvina mouth. The full Ohthere page could not be fetched.

label: Ohthere to Hedeby
summary: Ohthere's month-long voyage down the Norwegian coast to the market at Skiringssal (Kaupang) and on to Hedeby, the first description of Norway as a long coastal land.
notes: Told at King Alfred's court; the Great Belt passage to Hedeby is assumed (Ohthere names Jutland and islands on his right and left).

label: Gunnbjorn's skerries
summary: Storm-driven Norse sailor who sighted islands (Gunnbjarnarsker) off east Greenland, the first European sighting of Greenland.
notes: Date approximate (early 10th century). Skerries possibly near Tasiilaq (Ammassalik); not described in the fetched page, which only covers Erik.

label: Rus' to the Caspian
summary: Rus' fleets reached the Caspian Sea by the Volga (and the Don portage) and raided its coasts from Baku to Abaskun and Gorgan.
notes: The 913 fleet of about 500 ships came via the Dnieper, Black Sea, Don and a portage to the Volga; the route plotted here is the upper Volga trade route used by the Rus' to Bulghar and Atil. Known chiefly from Arabic writers (al-Masudi), with echoes in Norse runestones and sagas.

label: al-Mas'udi: India
summary: Voyage to Sind (Mansura, Multan), Cambay, Saymur and Ceylon described in Muruj al-Dhahab.
notes: Exact itinerary uncertain; his claim to have sailed on to China is doubted.

label: al-Mas'udi: Zanj
summary: Sailed from Oman down the Somali and Zanj coast to Qanbalu (probably Pemba), the earliest firsthand Arabic account of the Swahili coast.
notes: Sailed with Omani and Sirafi shipmasters.

leader: Swahili coast trade to Sofala (Arabic accounts)
label: Swahili coast to Sofala
summary: The gold and ivory trade of the Swahili towns (Zanzibar, Kilwa) reaching south to Sofala of the Zanj, as reported by al-Mas'udi.
notes: Knowledge came from Swahili and Arab traders on the coast, whose towns were African foundations.

label: Ibn Fadlan
summary: Embassy from Baghdad via Bukhara and Khwarazm across the Oghuz steppe to the Volga Bulgars, with the famous description of the Rus.
notes: Route between Khwarazm and the Volga (Ustyurt, Emba, Yaik crossings) is reconstructed.

label: Ibn Hawqal
summary: Thirty years of travel (943 to 973) from Iraq across North Africa to al-Andalus and Sijilmasa, extending Arabic description to the Sahara edge.
notes: Whether he reached Awdaghust himself is debated; he also described Sicily (973) and Transoxiana.

label: Rus' at Barda
summary: Rus' fleet sailed down the west Caspian coast and up the Kura river to seize Barda, the capital of Arran.

label: al-Muqaddasi
summary: Ahsan al-Taqasim (985), a systematic survey of every province of the Islamic world from personal travel.
notes: Order of travel reconstructed; he excludes Sind and al-Andalus, which he did not visit.

label: Erik the Red
summary: During three years of exile Erik explored the south-west coast of Greenland and chose the fjords that became the Norse settlements.
notes: Wintered and later settled at Brattahlid in Eriksfjord (inner fjord not plotted). Exiled from Iceland c. 982; returned 985/986 with settlers. Approach along the east coast and round Cape Farewell follows Landnamabok; the northern limit of his exploration is uncertain.

label: Bjarni
summary: Bjarni, blown off course sailing for Greenland, sighted three unknown lands to the west, the first recorded European sighting of North America.
notes: Greenland Saga only; the lands are commonly read as Newfoundland or southern Labrador, Labrador and Baffin Island. Route a reconstruction. Knowledge lost to Europe after the end of Norse Greenland.

label: Norse Greenland
summary: The Eastern and Western Settlements of Norse Greenland and their summer hunting grounds (Nordrsetur) north to Disko Bay and Upernavik, where a runestone of c. 1300 was found.
notes: Western Settlement abandoned c. 1360 (Ivar Bardarson found it empty); last news of the Eastern Settlement is the Hvalsey wedding of 1408 (visitors home 1410); end usually put c. 1450. Kingittorsuaq runestone near Upernavik (c. 1300). Inuit (Thule people) knew all these coasts.

label: Leif Erikson
summary: Leif sailed to Helluland (Baffin Island), Markland (Labrador) and Vinland, wintering at Leifsbudir, probably in northern Newfoundland.
notes: Followed Bjarni's report in reverse. L'Anse aux Meadows (found 1960) is the only confirmed Norse site; tree rings date wood cut there to 1021. Vinland survived in the sagas and in Adam of Bremen but was effectively lost to European geography.

label: Polynesian Outliers
summary: Polynesian voyagers sailed back west to settle Tuvalu and the Outliers such as Tikopia, Rennell, Ontong Java, Kapingamarangi and Nukuoro.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Dates vary by island (c. AD 1000 to 1500); order of settlement uncertain.

label: Karlsefni
summary: Karlsefni's attempt to settle Vinland with about 160 people explored south into the Gulf of St Lawrence (Straumfjord and Hop) before conflict with the Skraelings ended it.
notes: Erik the Red's Saga. Dates c. 1009 to 1012 not given in the fetched page. Butternuts found at L'Anse aux Meadows show Norse reached the southern Gulf of St Lawrence. Their son Snorri was the first European child born in America.

label: al-Biruni
summary: Followed the Ghaznavid court to Ghazni and the Punjab; measured the earth at Nandana and learned Sanskrit for his Kitab al-Hind (1030).

label: Society Islands
summary: The first settlement of East Polynesia, in the Society Islands (Tahiti, Raiatea), after the long pause in Samoa and Tonga.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. AD 1025 to 1120 (Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS, high-precision radiocarbon). Older chronologies proposed AD 300 to 900.

label: Kitab al-Hind
summary: Northern India from the Punjab to the Ganges and Malwa, described from Sanskrit learning in al-Biruni's India.
notes: Based on Indian pandits and texts; the far south is only lightly known.

label: Ingvar
summary: Large Swedish expedition east to Serkland (the Muslim lands round the Caspian) that ended in disaster in 1041, commemorated on some 26 Ingvar runestones.
notes: Route (Novgorod, Volga, Caspian, Georgia) is reconstructed from Yngvars saga and runestones; the fetched page does not describe it.

label: al-Bakri: Ghana
summary: Book of Roads and Kingdoms describing Awdaghust, Takrur, Silla, the royal town of Ghana, Kawkaw (Gao) and Tadmekka.
notes: Al-Bakri never travelled; he compiled reports from merchants and earlier writers (Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Warraq). Timbuktu itself was founded later.

label: Adam of Bremen's North
summary: Adam of Bremen's history (c. 1075) described the Baltic, Sweden, Norway to Halogaland, the Gulf of Bothnia, Estonia, Iceland, Greenland and, for the first time in a European book, Vinland.
notes: Informed at the court of Sweyn II Estridsson of Denmark and by missionaries. Vinland itself is not included in this base area because it remained hearsay; see leif-1000.

leader: First Crusade (Godfrey of Bouillon and others)
label: First Crusade
summary: Crusader armies marched from the Rhineland down the Danube to Constantinople and across Anatolia to Antioch and Jerusalem, and their chronicles gave Western readers first-hand geography of Anatolia and Syria.
notes: Godfrey's Danube route shown; other armies came via Italy and the Adriatic. Nicaea and Dorylaeum 1097, Antioch taken 1098, Jerusalem 15 July 1099. Guided across Anatolia by Byzantine troops under Tatikios and by Armenian Christians.

label: Baldwin to Edessa
summary: Baldwin left the main army, crossed the Euphrates and took Edessa, founding the first crusader state in upper Mesopotamia.
notes: Turbessel (Tell Bashir) and the Euphrates crossing; invited by the Armenian ruler Thoros.

label: Contact with the Americas
summary: Contact with the Pacific coast of South America, attested by the pre-Columbian sweet potato in Polynesia and by Native American DNA in East Polynesians.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Ioannidis et al. 2020 (Nature) date admixture to c. AD 1150 to 1230, earliest in Fatu Hiva, from a group related to the Zenu of Colombia. Direction of travel is unknown.

label: al-Idrisi: Africa
summary: The Sahel from Takrur to Kanem, Nubia, Abyssinia and the east African coast to Sofala as shown on the Tabula Rogeriana.

label: al-Idrisi: Europe
summary: Western, northern and eastern Europe (Britain, Norway, the Baltic, Poland, Rus) charted for Roger II from informants at Palermo.
notes: Compiled in Norman Sicily from travellers and older works; it circulated mainly in Arabic.

label: Benjamin of Tudela
summary: Benjamin's itinerary described some 300 cities from Spain through Italy, Greece, Constantinople, the Levant, Baghdad and Persia to Egypt, with hearsay of Arabia, India and China.
notes: Usually dated 1165 to 1173; the fetched page gives departure 1160. Which eastern places he saw and which he described from Jewish informants is disputed; the return across Arabia and via Sicily is a reconstruction.

label: Ibn Jubayr: to Alexandria
summary: Sailed on a Genoese ship from Ceuta past Sardinia, Sicily and Crete to Alexandria in 1183.

label: Ibn Jubayr: Mecca to Acre
summary: Up the Nile and across the Red Sea to Mecca, then by the pilgrim caravan to Baghdad, Mosul, Aleppo, Damascus and Crusader Acre.
notes: Red Sea crossing from Aydhab to Jeddah by boat.

label: Ibn Jubayr: return
summary: From Acre on a Christian ship, wrecked at Messina, through Norman Sicily to Cartagena in 1185.

leader: Settlement of the Austral Islands and Rapa
label: Australs, Rapa
summary: Settlement of Rurutu, Tubuai, Raivavae and remote Rapa Iti south of Tahiti.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. AD 1190 to 1290 pulse (Wilmshurst et al. 2011); Rapa somewhat later (c. AD 1200 to 1300, Kennett et al.).

label: Cook Islands
summary: Settlement of the southern Cook Islands (Aitutaki, Rarotonga, Mangaia) from the Society Islands.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Part of the AD 1190 to 1290 pulse of Wilmshurst et al. 2011; some argue for c. AD 1000.

label: Marquesas
summary: Settlement of the Marquesas via the Tuamotus, later a hub for voyages to Hawaii and Rapa Nui.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. AD 1190 to 1290 pulse (Wilmshurst et al. 2011); other estimates c. AD 1000 to 1100.

label: Pitcairn, Henderson
summary: Small Pitcairn and Henderson were settled from Mangareva and traded stone and shell with it.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Both islands were abandoned by c. 1450 to 1600 as the Mangareva trade collapsed (Weisler); lost gives an approximate abandonment year.

leader: Settlement of the Tuamotus and Mangareva
label: Tuamotus, Mangareva
summary: Atolls of the Tuamotus and the high islands of Mangareva (Gambier), a gateway to Pitcairn and Rapa Nui.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. AD 1190 to 1290 pulse (Wilmshurst et al. 2011).

label: Svalbard found
summary: Icelandic annals record 'Svalbard found' in 1194, a land four days' sail north of Iceland, probably Jan Mayen or the east coast of Greenland.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. The identification with modern Svalbard (Spitsbergen) is unlikely; plotted towards Jan Mayen. Knowledge did not survive.

label: Rapa Nui
summary: Settlement of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), the eastern apex of the Polynesian triangle.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. c. AD 1200 (Hunt and Lipo 2006; Wilmshurst et al. 2011 AD 1190 to 1293). Probably settled from Mangareva or the Marquesas.

label: Hawaii
summary: Settlement of the Hawaiian Islands, probably from the Marquesas and later in contact with Tahiti (Kahiki).
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. AD 1219 to 1266 (Wilmshurst et al. 2011); Athens et al. (2014) argue for c. AD 940 to 1130. Nihoa and Necker were used and later abandoned.

label: Changchun
summary: Daoist master who crossed Mongolia, the Altai and the Tian Shan to Samarkand and met Genghis Khan in the Hindu Kush; recorded in Xiyou ji.
notes: Account written by his disciple Li Zhichang; returned 1223 by a similar route.

label: Zhu Fan Zhi
summary: Song customs inspector Zhao Rugua described foreign lands from the Philippines and Java to India, Arabia, Zanzibar, Egypt, Sicily and the Maghreb.
notes: Compiled from Arab and Persian merchants at Quanzhou, with material from Zhou Qufei (1178).

leader: Giovanni da Pian del Carpine (with Benedict the Pole)
label: Plano Carpini
summary: Franciscan envoy who crossed the steppe from Kiev via Batu's camp on the Volga to the Mongol court near Karakorum, writing the first European account of the Mongols and Inner Asia.
notes: Left Lyon 16 April 1245; Batu's camp April 1246; Sira Orda 22 July 1246; Guyuk enthroned 24 August 1246; back at Kiev 10 June 1247. Benedict the Pole served as companion and interpreter; Mongol relay stations carried them. Steppe route between the Ural and Dzungaria approximate.

label: Aotearoa
summary: The last large land mass settled by humans, reached via the Kermadecs; earliest sites such as Wairau Bar date to the late 13th century.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. c. AD 1250 to 1300 (Wilmshurst et al. 2008, rat-gnawed seeds; 2011). Raoul Island in the Kermadecs was also settled and later abandoned. Route crosses the antimeridian.

label: Rubruck
summary: Franciscan who travelled from Constantinople across the Crimea and steppe to Mongke Khan at Karakorum and back via Derbent and Armenia; his report first told Europe that the Caspian is a lake and that Cathay was the land of the Seres.
notes: Source page could not be fetched in this session (fetch/search limits); route and dates from standard accounts, verify. Slightly beyond the 1250 cut-off but requested. Return through Sarai, Derbent, Nakhchivan, Erzurum, Sivas, Konya to Lajazzo (Ayas) and Tripoli. Relied on Mongol guides and an unreliable dragoman.

label: Marco Polo
summary: Gave Europe its first detailed description of the Silk Road through Persia, the Pamirs, the Tarim Basin and the Hexi corridor to Kublai Khan's court.
notes: Overland leg from Acre to Shangdu. Route between Hormuz and the Pamirs reconstructed from Il Milione. Knowledge of overland Cathay faded after the fall of the Yuan (1368); Goes (1605) confirmed Cathay was China.

label: Bar Sauma: to Persia
summary: Two Uyghur or Ongud monks from Khanbaliq crossed the Tarim and Khurasan to the Ilkhanate at Maragheh and Baghdad.
notes: Bar Sauma was born near Khanbaliq; his account, written in Persian and preserved in Syriac, reached Church of the East readers, not a Chinese audience.

label: Polo in China
summary: Described the interior of China from Khanbaliq to Yunnan and the Burmese border, and south through Hangzhou to Zaitun (Quanzhou).
notes: Composite of Polo's missions as described in Il Milione; order and dates reconstructed. Sea voyage Zaitun to Hormuz (1292-93) is handled by the sea-voyages file.

label: Bar Sauma: Europe
summary: First known person from China to reach western Europe: Constantinople, Naples, Rome, Genoa, Paris (Philip IV) and Gascony (Edward I).
notes: Sea legs Trebizond to Constantinople to Naples; viewpoint china by birth, see note on bar-sauma-1275-a.

label: Vivaldi brothers
summary: Two Genoese galleys sailed out through the Strait of Gibraltar and down the Moroccan Atlantic coast seeking India by sea, and vanished.
notes: Organised with Tedisio Doria; two Franciscan friars aboard. Last reported passing Gozora (Cape Nun, c. 28 47 N); nothing more was heard.

label: Polo return
summary: Return overland from Hormuz through Persia to Tabriz and Trebizond on the Black Sea.
notes: Hormuz to Trebizond; intermediate Persian towns assumed.

label: Zhou Daguan
summary: Yuan embassy from Wenzhou along the coast of Champa to the Mekong mouth; his Customs of Cambodia is the only eyewitness account of Angkor at its height.

label: Zhou Daguan: to Angkor
summary: Up the Mekong and Tonle Sap to Yasodharapura (Angkor), where he lived for about a year.

leader: Polynesian visit to the Auckland Islands
label: Auckland Islands
summary: Southernmost known Polynesian site, on Enderby Island in the subantarctic Auckland Islands, about 465 km south of New Zealand.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. 13th to 14th century occupation (Anderson and O'Regan 2003); abandoned after a short stay.

label: Kermadecs
summary: Raoul Island, a stepping stone between East Polynesia and New Zealand, was briefly occupied.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Occupation c. 14th century (Anderson); abandoned before European arrival.

label: Norfolk Island
summary: Norfolk Island had a Polynesian settlement at Emily Bay, probably from the Kermadecs or New Zealand, abandoned before 1774.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. Occupied c. 13th to 15th centuries (Anderson and White 2001).

label: Malocello
summary: Genoese navigator who reached Lanzarote, the first of the Canaries to reappear on a European map (Dulcert, 1339).
notes: Date 1312 is traditional; he reportedly lived on Lanzarote for close to two decades until expelled by a revolt of the islanders. A claimed 1336 Portuguese-sponsored return voyage is rejected by most historians.

label: Odoric
summary: Crossed Armenia and Persia from Trebizond via Tabriz, Sultaniyeh, Kashan, Yazd and Persepolis to Hormuz.
notes: He also mentions Baghdad; order uncertain. Then sailed to India (sea file).

label: Odoric in China
summary: Travelled from Canton and Zaitun up through Fuzhou, Hangzhou and Nanjing and the Grand Canal to Khanbaliq, giving Europe a vivid account of south China.
notes: Return c. 1328-1329 overland through Mongolia or Shaanxi, perhaps Tibet and Kashmir, is too uncertain to map; claim to have visited Lhasa is disputed.

label: Ibn Battuta 1: to Mecca
summary: From Tangier along North Africa to Egypt, up the Nile to Aydhab, then through Palestine and Syria to Mecca.

label: Ibn Battuta 2: Iraq, Iran
summary: With the returning Iraqi hajj caravan to Najaf and Basra, then Isfahan, Shiraz, Baghdad, Tabriz and Mosul.

label: Ibn Battuta 3: East Africa
summary: Down the Red Sea to Aden and Zeila, along the Swahili coast to Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa, then back via Dhofar, Oman, Hormuz and Bahrain.
notes: Dates 1328 to 1330 or 1330 to 1332 depending on chronology.

label: Ibn Battuta 4: Anatolia, steppe
summary: Through Anatolia and across the Black Sea to the Golden Horde, to Constantinople and back, then via Khwarazm, Bukhara, Samarkand and Afghanistan to the Indus.
notes: His claimed side trip to Bulghar on the Volga is doubted and omitted.

label: Wang Dayuan
summary: Two merchant voyages whose Daoyi Zhilue (1349) described about 100 places from Temasek (Singapore) to India, Hormuz and the Somali coast.
notes: Exact itinerary uncertain; some places may be described from hearsay.

label: Ibn Battuta 5: Sind to Delhi
summary: Sind and Multan to Delhi, where he served Muhammad bin Tughluq, then south through Malwa and Daulatabad to Cambay.

label: Marignolli
summary: Papal embassy across the Golden Horde and Chagatai steppes via Sarai, Almaliq and Hami to Khanbaliq.
notes: Sarai, Almaliq and Kumul (Hami) named in sources; Urgench, Otrar and Gobi points interpolated. Return 1347-1353 by sea via Quilon and Ceylon, then Hormuz, Baghdad, Aleppo, Damascus (not mapped here).

leader: Niccoloso da Recco and Angiolino del Tegghia de Corbizzi
label: Recco 1341
summary: Three-ship Portuguese-sponsored expedition that spent five months mapping thirteen islands of the Canaries.
notes: Brought four islanders back to Lisbon; Portugal later used the voyage to claim priority. Order of islands visited is reconstructed.

label: Ibn Battuta 6: Malabar, Maldives, Bengal
summary: Down the Malabar coast to Calicut, then the Maldives (where he served as qadi), Ceylon and Adam's Peak, Ma'bar and Bengal.

label: Ibn Battuta 7: to China
summary: From Bengal via Samudra (Sumatra) and the South China Sea to Zaitun (Quanzhou) and Guangzhou.
notes: His claimed visits to Hangzhou and Khanbaliq (Beijing) are doubted; 'Tawalisi' is unidentified.

label: Ibn Battuta 8: return to Hormuz
summary: Back from China via Sumatra, Quilon and Calicut across the Arabian Sea to Dhofar and Hormuz.

label: Ibn Battuta 9: home via Mecca
summary: Through Iran, Iraq and Syria during the Black Death to a last hajj at Mecca, then Cairo and Alexandria before sailing west to Fez (1349).
notes: From Alexandria he went by sea to Tunis and Sardinia and overland to Fez in late 1349.

label: Ibn Battuta 10: al-Andalus
summary: Across the strait to Gibraltar, Ronda, Malaga and Nasrid Granada.

label: Ibn Battuta 11: Mali
summary: Across the Sahara via Taghaza and Walata to the capital of Mali, then Timbuktu, Gao and Takedda and back north via Tuwat.
notes: Location of the Mali capital is uncertain (possibly on the upper Niger).

leader: Jean de Bethencourt and Gadifer de La Salle
label: Bethencourt
summary: Norman conquest of Lanzarote, Fuerteventura and El Hierro, described in the chronicle Le Canarien.
notes: Le Canarien was compiled by the chaplains Pierre Bontier and Jean Le Verrier; Gadifer's version is considered more reliable.

label: Clavijo
summary: Castilian embassy to Timur, describing the road from Trebizond through Persia and Khorasan to Samarkand.
notes: Return 1404-1406 via Bukhara, Karabakh and Tabriz, largely over the same Persian roads.

label: Isalguier (claimed)
summary: A Toulousain said to have lived eight years at Gao on the Niger and returned with an African wife, but his writings had no effect on European maps.
notes: Claim known only from later Toulouse family tradition; route to Gao unknown, so only Gao is plotted. His manuscripts (incl. a word list) were lost.

label: Zheng He 1
summary: Treasure fleet to Champa, Java, Palembang, Malacca, Semudera, Ceylon and Calicut.
notes: Accounts by Ma Huan, Fei Xin and Gong Zhen (later voyages); routes summarised on the Mao Kun map.

label: Zheng He 2
summary: Second fleet visited Siam as well as Java, Malacca, Ceylon, Cochin and Calicut.

label: Zheng He 3
summary: Third voyage to Calicut; on the way home the fleet fought and captured the king of Kotte in Ceylon (1411).
notes: The Galle trilingual inscription dates from 1409.

label: Zheng He 4
summary: First fleet beyond India, reaching Hormuz at the mouth of the Persian Gulf.
notes: Ma Huan, Muslim interpreter, sailed on this voyage and wrote Yingya Shenglan.

label: Chen Cheng
summary: Ming embassy to Shahrukh at Herat via Turfan, the Ili, Tashkent and Samarkand; recorded in Xiyu Fanguo Zhi.
notes: Accompanied by Li Xian; route north of the Tian Shan reconstructed.

label: Zheng He 5
summary: Fleet and detachments reached Hormuz, Aden and the east African ports of Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi.
notes: Detachment routes simplified into one track.

leader: Joao Goncalves Zarco, Tristao Vaz Teixeira, Bartolomeu Perestrelo
label: Zarco
summary: Portuguese caravels recognised Porto Santo and then Madeira, settled from 1425.
notes: The islands appear on some 14th-century portolans, so this is a rediscovery and first settlement.

label: Conti
summary: Crossed the Syrian desert from Damascus to Baghdad and went down the Tigris to Basra.
notes: Desert route via Palmyra assumed. His account was taken down by Poggio Bracciolini and fed Fra Mauro's map.

label: Conti in India
summary: Went inland from Cambay to the city of Vijayanagar and across the peninsula to Mylapore.
notes: Route between named places reconstructed.

label: Zheng He 6
summary: Returned foreign envoys home; detachments visited Dhofar, Aden, Mogadishu and Brava.

label: Conti in Burma
summary: From Bengal to Arakan and overland to Ava and Pegu, the first European account of Burma's interior.
notes: Years approximate (early 1420s).

label: Silves
summary: Portuguese pilot credited with finding the eastern and possibly central Azores.
notes: Date read from a smudged note on Vallseca's 1439 map: 1427, 1432 or 1437. Flores and Corvo were probably not reached.

label: Goncalo Velho
summary: Found the Formigas rocks and Santa Maria, beginning the official Portuguese discovery of the Azores.
notes: His crew later sighted Sao Miguel on 8 May 1444; settlement of Santa Maria began 1439.

label: Zheng He 7
summary: Last voyage to Hormuz; a detachment with Ma Huan sailed up the Red Sea to Jeddah for Mecca.
notes: Zheng He died in 1433, probably near Calicut, on the return.

label: Gil Eanes
summary: First recorded European ship to pass Cape Bojador and return, opening the Saharan coast.
notes: Returned by a volta do mar, bringing wild plants as proof of landing.

leader: Gil Eanes and Afonso Goncalves Baldaia
label: Angra dos Ruivos
summary: Sailed 30 to 50 leagues beyond Bojador to the bay they named Angra dos Ruivos.

label: Baldaia
summary: Named the Rio do Ouro inlet (Dakhla) and crossed the Tropic of Cancer to Pedra da Gale off Cape Barbas.

label: Nuno Tristao 1441
summary: Reached Cape Blanc (Ras Nouadhibou).

label: Nuno Tristao 1443
summary: Reached the Bay of Arguin and Arguin island.

label: Nuno Tristao 1445
summary: Reached the Langue de Barbarie near the mouth of the Senegal River, the edge of the Sahel.
notes: Dates of the third and fourth voyages are uncertain (1444 to 1447).

label: Nuno Tristao 1446
summary: Passed Cap Vert to a large river, probably in the Sine-Saloum delta, where he was killed.
notes: Dates of the third and fourth voyages are uncertain (1444 to 1447).

label: Malfante
summary: Genoese merchant whose 1447 letter from the Tuat oasis gave Europe its first eyewitness report of the Sahara trade and hearsay of Timbuktu and the Niger.
notes: Letter written at Tuat (Tamentit). Landing at Honein and route via Tlemcen are the usual reconstruction, not stated in the source read.

label: Chatham Islands
summary: Moriori ancestors from New Zealand settled the Chatham Islands, 800 km east of the mainland.
notes: Settlement date from archaeology and radiocarbon, not a written account. c. AD 1450 to 1650; earlier estimates c. AD 1500. Route crosses the antimeridian.

label: Cadamosto 1455
summary: Venetian in Henry's service who described Senegal, Cayor and the Gambia mouth in his widely printed Navigazioni.
notes: Spent a month inland in Cayor. The Navigazioni was printed in 1507 (Paesi novamente retrovati) and translated into Latin, German and French.

label: Cadamosto 1456
summary: Reported the Cape Verde Islands (Boa Vista, Santiago), went up the Gambia to Badibu and on to the Geba estuary and Bissagos.
notes: Some historians doubt the 1456 Cape Verde discovery date and parts of the account.

label: Cadamosto up the Gambia
summary: Sailed about 60 Italian miles up the Gambia to visit the ruler he called Battimansa in Badibu.
notes: Stayed 11 days until malaria struck the crew.

label: Diogo Gomes 1456
summary: Reached the Rio Grande (Geba) and then sailed some 50 leagues up the Gambia to the Mali gold market of Cantor.
notes: Date c. 1456.

label: Gomes up the Gambia
summary: Went about 50 leagues up the Gambia to Cantor, a market town for Mali gold.
notes: Cantor (Kuntaur area) location approximate.

leader: Diogo Gomes and Antonio de Noli
label: Diogo Gomes 1462
summary: Traded in the Saloum delta and landed on and named Santiago in the Cape Verde Islands.
notes: Possibly 1460. Cadamosto disputes his priority for Cape Verde.

label: Ibn Majid
summary: Kitab al-Fawa'id (c. 1490), a pilot's manual of Indian Ocean sea routes, star altitudes and coasts from the Gulf to Malacca.
notes: His works also cover the Red Sea, East Africa and Madagascar; the story that he piloted Vasco da Gama is now generally rejected.

label: Pedro de Sintra
summary: Charted the coast of Sierra Leone and Liberia past Cape Mount and Cape Mesurado to the Bosco de Santa Maria.
notes: Turned back because his interpreters could not understand the local language. His voyage is reported in Cadamosto's Navigazioni.

label: Nikitin
summary: From Tver down the Volga, round the Caspian and across Persia to Hormuz, the first Russian account of the route to India.
notes: Dates follow Semyonov's revised chronology (departure 1468); traditional dating 1466-1472.

label: Nikitin in India
summary: Described the Deccan interior: Junnar, the Bahmani capital Bidar and the shrine of Parvattum.
notes: Parvattum identified with Srisailam; exit port assumed Dabhol.

label: Fernao do Po
summary: First European to reach Bioko (Formosa, later Fernando Po) and the Cameroon coast at the head of the Gulf of Guinea.

label: Nikitin return
summary: Returned from Hormuz across Persia and eastern Anatolia to Trebizond, then from Caffa north towards Smolensk, where he died.
notes: Persian stages between Hormuz and Trebizond assumed; Trebizond to Caffa by sea.

label: Diogo Cao I
summary: Found the mouth of the Congo and followed the Angolan coast to Cabo de Santa Maria, setting stone padroes.
notes: Traded with the Bakongo near the river mouth.

label: Diogo Cao II
summary: Second voyage carrying the coast survey on to Cabo Negro and Cape Cross in Namibia.
notes: Fate after Cape Cross uncertain.

label: Cão up the Congo
summary: Portuguese boats ascended the Congo estuary to the Yellala falls, leaving a carved inscription, the first European penetration of the river.
notes: Yellala inscription date (1485 or 1487) is debated. Wikipedia article could not be fetched in this session (access blocked); route and dates from general knowledge, verify.

leader: Pero da Covilha and Afonso de Paiva
label: Covilha (Egypt)
summary: Royal spies sent to find the spice routes and Prester John crossed Egypt from Alexandria via Cairo to the Red Sea.
notes: Left Santarem 7 May 1487 via Barcelona, Naples and Rhodes; Nile boat to Cairo then caravan to the Red Sea.

label: Covilha (Indian Ocean)
summary: Travelling on Arab and Indian trading vessels he saw Aden, Calicut, Goa, Hormuz and the Swahili coast to Sofala, reporting the Indian Ocean trade to Lisbon.
notes: Relied on Muslim and Indian merchants and their dhows. Exact sea paths between named ports are reconstructed; his report reached Lisbon via Jose Sapateiro.

label: Bartolomeu Dias
summary: Rounded the southern tip of Africa unseen, landed at Mossel Bay, reached Kwaaihoek and sighted the Cape of Good Hope on the way home.
notes: Padrao de Sao Gregorio at Kwaaihoek near the Boesmans River marked the furthest point.

label: Sousa to Mbanza Kongo
summary: Portuguese embassy marched from Mpinda at the Congo mouth to the Kongo capital Mbanza Kongo, opening the kingdom to European description.
notes: Wikipedia article could not be fetched in this session (access blocked); route and dates from general knowledge, verify.

label: Columbus I
summary: First European crossing to the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, opening the Caribbean to European knowledge.
notes: Landfall at Guanahani (San Salvador, identification debated); Taino captives taken as interpreters.

label: Covilhã
summary: Portuguese envoy who, after scouting Cairo, Aden, India and Sofala, went inland from Zeila to the Ethiopian court and never left.
notes: Source places the Ethiopian trip after his 1491 return to Cairo without a year. His knowledge reached Europe via letters and via Francisco Álvares, who met him in 1520. Sea legs (Red Sea, India, Sofala) belong to the coastal dataset.

label: Covilha to Zeila
summary: After revisiting Aden, Hormuz and Jeddah he crossed the Red Sea from Sinai to Zeila on the Somali coast.
notes: Accompanied part of the way by Rabbi Abraham of Beja. Year approximate.

label: Columbus II
summary: Charted the Lesser Antilles, Puerto Rico, Jamaica and the south coast of Cuba.

label: Covilha to Ethiopia
summary: Went inland from Zeila to the court of the Ethiopian emperor Eskender, where he spent the rest of his life.
notes: Inland route and court location (Shewa) reconstructed. Found there by the Portuguese embassy of Rodrigo de Lima in 1520.

label: Cabot
summary: English landfall in Newfoundland, the first recorded European visit to mainland North America since the Norse.
notes: Landfall disputed (Cape Bonavista, St. John's, Labrador or Cape Breton suggested); extent of coast explored unknown.

label: Vasco da Gama
summary: First sea voyage from Europe to India, charting the Natal and Swahili coasts and crossing the Arabian Sea to Calicut.
notes: At Malindi he took on a Gujarati pilot who knew the monsoon route. Natal named at Christmas 1497.

label: Columbus III
summary: First European sighting of the South American mainland at Trinidad, the Gulf of Paria and the Orinoco outflow.

leader: Alonso de Ojeda, Juan de la Cosa, Amerigo Vespucci
label: Ojeda
summary: Followed the Venezuelan coast from the Orinoco to the Guajira, naming the Gulf of Venezuela and Lake Maracaibo.
notes: Wayuu stilt villages gave Venezuela its name; Vespucci may have split off south toward Brazil.

label: Pinzon
summary: First European landfall in Brazil and first entry into the Amazon estuary, the 'Mar Dulce'.
notes: Landfall disputed between Cabo de Santo Agostinho and Ceara.

label: Cabral
summary: Second India fleet: made the first recorded European landfall in Brazil (Monte Pascoal, Porto Seguro), then reached Sofala, Kilwa, Calicut and Cochin.
notes: A supply ship carried news of Brazil back to Lisbon. Bartolomeu Dias drowned when four ships were lost off the Cape.

label: Diogo Dias
summary: Separated from Cabral, he sighted Madagascar (Sao Lourenco), sailed past Cape Guardafui into the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea mouth.
notes: Forced aground on the Eritrean coast and attacked before escaping; met Cabral's fleet at Bezeguiche (Dakar) in June 1501. Return path reconstructed.

label: Vespucci
summary: Followed the Brazilian coast south to Rio de Janeiro and Cananeia, convincing Vespucci it was a new continent.
notes: Vespucci's claim of reaching 52 S is disputed and not plotted.

label: Joao da Nova
summary: Third India fleet, credited with finding Ascension on the way out and St Helena on the way home.
notes: St Helena date traditionally 21 May 1502 (via Linschoten), perhaps 3 May; a 2022 review doubts Nova found St Helena at all.

label: Columbus IV
summary: Coasted Central America from Honduras to Panama, adding the Caribbean shore of the isthmus to the map.
notes: Met a Maya trading canoe off Guanaja; marooned in Jamaica 1503 to 1504.

leader: Estevao da Gama's squadron of Vasco da Gama's 4th India fleet (account by Thome Lopes)
label: Thome Lopes
summary: Eyewitness account of the 1502 to 1503 India voyage, describing St Helena as an unknown island on 30 July 1503 and mentioning Ascension.
